tagline: Spec-driven planning layer: Plan → Execute → Verify.

phases.label: Epic Mode
phases.note: Interviews you about problem, stack, edge cases → generates PRDs, specs, tech flows, wireframes, sequence diagrams.

phases.label: Plan
phases.note: Sequences the objective into phases; each phase gets a file-by-file plan (classes, variables, call hierarchies).

phases.label: Execute
phases.note: Hands each phase to the agent of your choice — Cursor, Claude Code, Copilot.

phases.label: Verify
phases.note: Acceptance checks tied to intent + tests + static analysis + diff-level reasoning; fix-forward on regressions.

scenarios.note: Skip Epic Mode; a quick plan → dispatch handles it, though it's still a planning layer over the agent.
Epic Mode (PRDs, specs, wireframes → agent-sized tickets) is **built for 0→1**.
File-by-file plans across files plus verification suit cross-file refactors.
Lightweight plan → dispatch → verify; faster than heavyweight IDE spec flows.
Sequential phases dispatched to one agent — **no parallel isolation**.
File-by-file planning enumerates every site; verify catches per-form regressions.

keyFeatures: Sits on top of Cursor / Claude Code / Copilot — bring your own agent
Plan → Execute → Verify loop with acceptance checks tied to intent
Epic Mode: interview → PRDs, specs, tech flows, wireframes → agent-sized tickets
File-by-file plans (classes, variables, call hierarchies) per phase
Persistent plan as a ticket system (vs a one-shot document)
100K+ users; credit-based tiers (Free / Lite / Pro / Ultra)
limitations: Proprietary, closed-source VS Code extension (no public repo)
Credit-based pricing; heavy parallel use burns credits fast
No parallel multi-agent isolation — phases run sequentially
VS Code-centric; output quality depends on the underlying agent
Mini-specs are work artifacts, not a maintained living spec
